history.title: Crew Launch Week 8: Small Moves, Not Big Speeches

data.body:
Crew slot: 40 minutes. HOWL: Respect. "I am a respectful member of the King community."

This week is about the small moves that change a lunch table, and about making one of them.

1. Read **Small Moves, Not Big Speeches** (10 minutes).
2. Learn the **Glossary** words, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Bystander or Upstander?** chart open.
4. Sort the cards in **Small Move, Big Speech, or Get an Adult?**
5. Take the quiz. Question 3 is about Jae at the lunch table.
6. Open the SEL Hub and choose [Upstander Training](#sel-hub/upstander?station=sel_station_crew_launch_upstander). Read the courage ladder in Moves and pick two moves you could actually make. Then open [Peer Support Coach](#sel-hub/peersupport?station=sel_station_crew_launch_upstander) for the words to use afterwards with the person who was left out.
7. Use the **Sentence Frames** to write your two small moves and when you would use them.
8. Lock it in with **Remember Notice, Move, Check**.
9. Finish with the **Design Challenge: Our Crew's Invite Signal**.

Your commitment: this week, make one small move when someone is left out or talked over, and bring back what happened. 🤝

Clicking a tool link above also starts your Crew station for this week, so the time you spend in the tools and the self-check stay together in one place. It stays active until you exit it, so come back later in the week to mark the self-check. You can find it again under SEL Stations in the History panel. 📌

history.title: Small Moves, Not Big Speeches
history.data:
## Small Moves, Not Big Speeches

**HOWL: "I am a respectful member of the King community."**

Everyone knows what a **bystander** is. Someone is being left out, talked over, or picked on, and a ring of people watch it happen. Almost nobody in that ring is cruel. Most of them are waiting for someone else to move first, or they are afraid that moving will make it worse, or they simply do not know what a move would look like. Researchers have a name for the waiting: the **bystander effect**. The more people watching, the less likely any one of them is to act.

An **upstander** is not a hero with a speech. An upstander is someone who makes one **small move**. The move is usually about the size of a sentence. "Wait, I want to hear what she was saying." "Come sit with us." "That is not funny." Sometimes the move is not words at all: changing seats, starting a different conversation, catching someone's eye and nodding. Sometimes the move happens afterwards, in private, as a **check in**: "That was rough. You okay?"

Here is a moment from a fictional **Crew**. At lunch, Tomas is telling a story and Reyna keeps cutting across him with jokes. The table laughs at the jokes. Tomas gets quieter and finally stops. Nobody at the table thinks of themselves as unkind. Then Jae says, not loudly, "Hold on, Tomas, what happened next?" That is the whole move: a **redirect** back to Tomas. Reyna is not called out. Tomas finishes. The table has changed shape by one sentence.

Small moves work because they are **low risk**. A big speech makes the person being **excluded** into a **spectacle** and makes everyone else defensive. A small move keeps the situation ordinary. It also does something else: it shows the ring of watchers that moving is possible. The second move is usually easier than the first, and it is often made by someone who saw the first one.

Being a respectful member of a **community**, the King Respect **HOWL**, is mostly made of these moments. Not the assembly about kindness. The lunch table. The group chat. The hallway. The moment when you could look away and do not.

Some situations are bigger than a small move. If someone is being hurt or threatened, or targeted again and again, the move is to get an adult, and that is not tattling; it is the correct size of response. This week is about the everyday version: the exclusions and cut-offs that happen ten times a day and that one sentence can change.

history.title: Small Move, Big Speech, or Get an Adult?

categories.label: GET AN ADULT (bigger than a move)

items.content: Standing up at the table: "Everyone here needs to think about how they treat people."
Someone has been shoved into the same locker three days in a row.
Moving your tray to sit next to the person eating alone.
A group chat is sharing a photo of a classmate that they did not agree to.
Catching the eye of the person who got cut off and nodding.
Posting a long message in the chat about how everyone is being toxic.
Afterwards, quietly: "That was rough. You okay?"
A student says another student threatened to hurt them after school.
Telling the joker, in front of everyone, that they are a bully.

questions.question: What does the reading say about most people in the ring of watchers?
options: They enjoy watching someone else get picked on instead of them
They have already decided the person being picked on must deserve it
They are too far away from what is happening to do anything
They are waiting for someone else to move, or do not know what a move is
questions.correctAnswer: They are waiting for someone else to move, or do not know what a move is

questions.question: What is the bystander effect?
options: The more people watching, the less likely any one of them is to act
People become braver and more likely to help when there is a crowd
Watching someone get hurt makes you feel guilty about it for days
Adults are less likely to help than students
questions.correctAnswer: The more people watching, the less likely any one of them is to act

questions.question: What was Jae's move at the lunch table?
options: Jae told Reyna, "Stop being rude."
Jae asked the table to vote on who could talk
Jae said "Hold on, Tomas, what happened next?"
Jae left the table to find a teacher
questions.correctAnswer: Jae said "Hold on, Tomas, what happened next?"

questions.question: Why does the reading say a big speech usually works worse than a small move?
options: Because speeches take too long and lunch is short
Because it makes a spectacle and makes everyone else defensive
Because teachers do not like speeches in the lunchroom
Because the person making the jokes will just tell an even better one
questions.correctAnswer: Because it makes a spectacle and makes everyone else defensive

questions.question: Someone is being threatened after school. What size of response does the reading say fits?
options: Getting an adult, which is the correct size, not tattling
A small move, like quietly starting a different conversation
A speech to the person doing the threatening, in front of everyone
Waiting to see whether it happens again
questions.correctAnswer: Getting an adult, which is the correct size, not tattling

questions.question: Someone at lunch keeps getting talked over. Write one small move you could make in the next thirty seconds that does not require a speech.
questions.expectedAnswer: A small move: "Wait, I want to hear what she was saying," moving a seat, asking them a direct question, or checking in afterwards.

reflections.text: Think of a time you were in the ring. What small move would have been possible? What stopped it?

| Criteria | 1 - Starting | 3 - Getting There | 5 - Crew Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sentence-sized | A speech, or nothing | One action, a bit long | One sentence or one action anyone could make |
| Redirects, not accuses | Names the person doing the excluding | Mostly about the excluded person | Turns the moment back to the excluded person without a spectacle |
| Knows the limit | No line between a move and getting an adult | Names one situation that needs an adult | Names the situations that need an adult and why that is the right size |

data.question: What is Crew, anyway?
data.answer: Crew is your school's word for a small group of students and one adult who meet regularly to check in, set goals, and work through hard things together. It comes from EL Education, the school model King has used since 1992, and from an old idea about ships: everyone on board is crew, not a passenger. Read more on [King's EL page](https://king.portlandschools.org/about/learning-models) or [EL Education's Crew page](https://www.eleducation.org/crew).

data.question: What is a HOWL?
data.answer: A Habit of Work and Learning. Your school scores three of them, apart from your academic grades: Respect ("I am a respectful member of the King community"), Responsibility ("I take responsibility for my success as a learner"), and Perseverance ("I persevere to produce high quality work"). Teachers score them; Crew is where you practice them. The statements are on [King's grading guide](https://king.portlandschools.org/families/handbook/handbook-interior/~board/king-student-family-handbook/post/grading-guide).

data.question: What if I make a move and it makes things worse?
data.answer: Small moves rarely do; that is why they are small. "What happened next?" cannot really backfire. If a situation is the kind where any move might make it worse, that is your signal it is bigger than a move, and the move is an adult.

data.question: What if the person being picked on is someone I do not like?
data.answer: The move is still the move. You are not becoming their friend. You are keeping the table a place where being talked over is not normal, which protects you too.

data.question: Is getting an adult tattling?
data.answer: Tattling is trying to get someone in trouble for something small. Getting an adult when someone is hurt or threatened, or targeted again and again is the correct size of response. The reading is clear about the difference.

data.question: What if I froze and did nothing?
data.answer: Then you were in the ring, like most people most of the time. The afterwards move still exists: "That was rough. You okay?" It counts.

data.question: How does this connect to my HOWL grade?
data.answer: The Respect HOWL says you are a respectful member of the King community. A community is made at the lunch table, not at the assembly. Your teachers score HOWLs; Crew is where you practice them.

cards.target: Notice, make one small move, check in afterwards

cards.aiExample: Notice, Move, Check. Three beats, like a knock on a door: see it, say one thing, ask them later.
cards.mapping: Three beats in order keep the move small: you are not planning a speech, you are doing one thing now and one thing later.

history.title: Design Challenge: Our Crew's Invite Signal

data.title: Our Crew's Invite Signal
data.instructions: Design one small move your whole Crew agrees to use when someone is left out or cut off, test it for a week in and out of Crew, and revise it.
data.fitReason: The HOWL behavior is being a respectful member of the community. A shared move the Crew designs and uses turns "be an upstander" into one agreed action, and the week of use shows whether it is small enough to actually happen.

brief.context: Your Crew has read about small moves. Individually, everyone has two. As a group, you do not yet have one that everyone recognizes. A shared signal is easier to make because everyone knows what it means and nobody has to be first alone.
brief.audience: Your Crew, and the tables and group chats where its members sit during the week
brief.drivingQuestion: What is one small move every member of our Crew could make when someone is left out, and does it actually get used?
brief.seedDirection: Brainstorm moves that are sentence-sized and low risk. Pick one for "talked over" and one for "sitting alone." Agree on the words. Use them for a week. Count how many times each one happened and what it was like.
lockedLessonFacts: Most people in the ring are waiting for someone else to move first.
An upstander makes one small move, about the size of a sentence.
A small move keeps the situation ordinary; a big speech makes a spectacle.
If someone is hurt or threatened, or targeted again and again, the move is to get an adult.
openQuestions: Which candidate moves are really speeches?
Where in the week will the move most likely be needed?
How will we count without making it a competition?
stakeholders: The Crew member most likely to be talked over
The Crew member most likely to be doing the talking over
Students outside the Crew at the same tables
criteria: Each move is one sentence or one action
Each move redirects to the excluded person without naming the excluder
The Crew names what is bigger than a move and who the adult is
The week's count is honest, including zero
Uses at least three glossary words in the record
constraints: Words agreed by the whole Crew
The revision changes at most one thing
brief.deliverable: A Crew card with the two moves in the agreed words, the "bigger than a move" line, and a one-week count with one revision.

parallelExample.context: A fictional Crew chose "Wait, I want to hear the end of that" for talked-over moments.
parallelExample.move: After a week the count was three. Two members said the words felt stiff. The revision was to shorten it to "Wait, what happened next?" which is what Jae said in the reading.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: It shows that a move too long to say gets shortened, not abandoned.

supports.frameStarter: When someone is talked over, we say "____." When someone is alone, we ____. It is bigger than a move when ____, and then we ____.
frameChoices: We used the first move ____ times this week.
The hardest moment to use it was ____.
coachPrompts: Would a quiet member of your Crew actually say these words?
Which move would you have wanted someone to make for you last year?

data.coachHint: If the count is zero, that is data, not failure. Ask whether the moments did not come up or whether the move was too big to make.
data.sourceExcerpt: An upstander is not a hero with a speech. An upstander is someone who makes one small move. The move is usually about the size of a sentence.
